en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 84, the Madhura Sutta.
On one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling at Madhurā in the Gundā Grove.
King Avantiputta of Madhurā heard:
"The ascetic Kaccāna, it is said, is dwelling at Madhurā in the Gundā Grove."
Moreover, this excellent report of the venerable Kaccāna has spread abroad:
"He is wise, discerning, intelligent, learned, an eloquent speaker, possessed of ready wit, aged, and an arahant.
Indeed, it is good to see such arahants."
Then King Mādhura, the son of Avantī, having had excellent carriages prepared,
mounted an excellent carriage and set out from Madhurā with great royal splendor in excellent carriages to see the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a carriage, he alighted from the carriage and approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna on foot.
Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Mādhura...
The son of Avantī said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
“Master Kaccāna, the brahmins say thus:
‘The brahmin caste alone is the highest caste; other castes are inferior;’”
‘Only the brahmin is the fair complexion; any other complexion is dark.
Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.
Only brahmins are the legitimate sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.’”
“In this regard, venerable Kaccāna, what do you declare?
“Great King, it is merely a report in the world:
‘The brahmin caste alone is the highest caste; other castes are inferior.’”
‘Only the brahmin is the fair complexion; any other complexion is dark.
Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.
Only brahmins are the legitimate sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.’”
This, great king, should be understood through a methodical exposition:
that this is merely a sound in the world, namely, “The brahmin alone is the highest caste; other castes are inferior...
[down to] the heirs of Brahmā.”
"What do you think, great king?

If a kshatriya were to succeed in wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would that kshatriya rise before him and retire after him, be obedient to his commands, act with agreeable conduct, and speak kindly? ...
"And would a brahmin also [do so] for him?"...
“Would his merchant also rise before him, retire after him, be obedient to his commands, act with agreeable conduct, and speak kindly? “If, Master Kaccāna,

a nobleman should succeed through wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would his nobleman also rise before him, retire after him, be obedient to his commands, act with agreeable conduct, and speak kindly?”

"A brahmin among them would also be one who rises before him and retires after him, who is obedient to his every command, who conducts himself agreeably, and who speaks kindly; so too would a merchant, and so too would a laborer."
“What do you think, great king?

Even if a brahmin were to succeed through wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would that brahmin still rise before him and retire after him, be attentive to his needs, act with kindness, and speak pleasant words?
… Would a merchant also [do so] for him?”
“Would even a pure person rise before him and retire after him, being one who accepts what is to be done, who acts agreeably, and who speaks kindly?

“If, Master Kaccāna, a brahmin were to prosper through wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would even that brahmin rise before him and retire after him, being one who accepts what is to be done, who acts agreeably, and who speaks kindly?”

“Perhaps a merchant will be his servant… perhaps a worker will be his servant… perhaps a noble will be his servant— rising before him, retiring after him, obedient to his every command, acting with agreeable conduct, and speaking kindly.”

“What do you think, great king? If a merchant were to succeed in wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would that merchant rise before him and retire after him, be attentive to his needs, act with agreeable conduct, and speak kindly?
“… Would a laborer also do so for him?
“… Would a noble also do so for him?”
“Would a brahmin also rise before him and retire after him, be one who accepts his instructions, behaves agreeably, and speaks kindly?

“If, Master Kaccāna, a merchant should succeed through wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would a merchant also rise before him and retire after him, be one who accepts his instructions, behaves agreeably, and speaks kindly?
… Would a worker also [do so] for him?”

“A kṣatriya might also be his [servant]… a brahmin might also be his [servant], rising before him and retiring after him, obedient to his every command, acting with agreeable conduct, and speaking kindly.

“What do you think, Great King? If even a *śūdra* were to succeed through wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would that *śūdra* also rise before him and retire after him, be obedient to his every command, act with agreeable conduct, and speak kindly?”

“Would a kshatriya also rise before her and retire after her, being one who responds to what is needed, acts agreeably, and speaks kindly? “Would a brahmin also rise before her and retire after her, being one who responds to what is needed, acts agreeably, and speaks kindly? “Would a vaisya also rise before her and retire after her, being one who responds to what is needed, acts agreeably, and speaks kindly?”

“Even if a *sudda*, Master Kaccāna, were to succeed through wealth, grain, silver, or gold, he would still be one who rises before [his master], retires after him, is obedient to his commands, behaves agreeably, and speaks kindly… even a *khattiya* would be such for him… even a *brāhmaṇa* would be such for him…”
“He would rise before him and retire after him; he would be one who accepts what is to be done, who acts agreeably, and who speaks kindly.
“What do you think, Great King, if this were so, would these four castes be equal and alike, or not?”
“And what do you think about this?
“Certainly, Master Kaccāna, that being so, these four castes are exactly equal.
I do not perceive any distinction between them here.”
“By this method also, Great King, it should be understood how this mere sound has arisen in the world:
‘The brahmin alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior...
[down to] the heirs of Brahmā.’”
"What do you think, great king?

Suppose here there were a kṣatriya who was a taker of life, a taker of what is not given, one of wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, a speaker of falsehood, a speaker of divisive speech, a speaker of harsh speech, a speaker of idle chatter, covetous, ill-willed, and of wrong view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he would [go] to a state of deprivation..."
"Would he be reborn in a state of misery, in a state of ruin, or in hell?
Or how do you regard this matter?
"For even a kshatriya, Master Kaccāna, who takes life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, and uses malicious speech..."
"One who speaks harshly, who indulges in idle chatter, who is covetous, whose mind is full of ill will, and who holds wrong view— upon the breakup of the body, after death,
might such a person be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell. This is my conviction in this matter,
and thus have I heard it from the Arahants."
“Excellent, excellent, great king!
It is well that you think thus, great king; it is well indeed that you have heard this from the Arahants.
What do you think, great king?”
"Suppose here there were a brahmin...
suppose here there were a merchant...

suppose here there were a worker who was a taker of life, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view; upon the breakup of the body, after death, would he not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, or in hell?"
“And what do you think about this?

“Even a pure person, Master Kaccāna, who has committed the destruction of life, taken what was not given... [and so on] ...up to having wrong view, might upon the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
This is how it occurs to me in this matter, and this is what I have heard from the Arahants.”
“Excellent, excellent, great king!
It is good that you think thus, great king, and it is good indeed that you have heard this from the Arahants.
What do you think, great king?”
“If this is so, are these four castes equal and alike, or not?
Or what do you think about this?
“Certainly, Master Kaccāna, if this is so, these four castes are equal and alike.”
“I do not perceive any difference between them in this regard.
“By this method also, Great King, it should be understood how this mere sound has arisen in the world:
‘The brahmin caste alone is the best; other castes are inferior... [down to] ...the heirs of Brahmā.’”
“What do you think, Great King?
Suppose here there were a noble who abstained from taking life, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct,
abstained from false speech, abstained from malicious speech, abstained from harsh speech, and abstained from idle chatter.”
Abstaining [from these], free from covetousness, with a mind devoid of ill will, and possessing right view, would such a person, upon the breakup of the body after death,
not be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world?
Or how do you stand on this matter?”
“Master Kaccāna, a khattiya as well who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct,
abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, abstains from idle chatter, who is without covetousness,
with a mind free from ill will, and who holds right view— upon the breakup of the body, after death...”
“Upon death, may I be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
Such is my thought in this matter, and thus have I heard it from the Arahants.
“Excellent, excellent, Great King!”
"It is good for you, Great King, that it is so; it is also good that you have heard this from the Arahants.
What do you think, Great King:

suppose here there were a brahmin, here a merchant, and here a worker, each abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given... [and so on] ...with right view. Upon the breakup of the body, after death, would they not be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world?"
“And what do you think about this?

“Master Kaccāna, even a pure person who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given... [and so on] ...and possesses right view might, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
This is how it occurs to me here, and this is what I have heard from the Arahants.”
“Excellent, excellent, Great King!
It is well that you think thus, Great King; it is well indeed that you have heard this from the Arahants.
What do you think, Great King?”
“If this is so, are these four castes equal and alike, or not?
Or what is your view on this?
“Certainly, Master Kaccāna, if this is so, these four castes are equal and alike.”
“I do not perceive any difference between them in this regard.
“By this method also, Great King, it should be understood how this mere sound has arisen in the world:
‘The brahmin caste alone is the best; other castes are inferior... [down to] ...the heirs of Brahmā.’”
“What do you think, great king?

Suppose here a noble were to break into a house, or carry off plunder, or commit burglary, or stand as an ambusher on the road, or go to another’s wife; and if men were to seize him and bring him before you, saying:
‘This man, sire, is a thief, a wrongdoer.’”
“Bet whatever wager you wish on this man.
“What would you do with him, Master Kaccāna? “We would have him executed, or we would have him imprisoned, or we would have him exiled, or we would deal with him according to the circumstances.”
"And for what reason?
Because, Master Kaccāna, that former designation of him as a ‘Khattiya’ has vanished; he is now reckoned simply as a thief.
“What do you think, Great King?”
Suppose here a brahmin, a merchant, or a worker were to break into a house,
plunder by ambush, commit a burglary, lie in wait on a highway, or commit adultery with another's wife;
and suppose those men were to seize him and bring him before you, saying:
‘Your Majesty, this is a thief, a criminal.
Inflict upon him whatever punishment you wish. What would you do with him?”
“We would have him executed, Master Kaccāna, or we would have him imprisoned, or we would have him banished, or we would deal with him according to the circumstances. And why is that?
Because, Master Kaccāna, whatever designation he previously had as a ‘Sudda’ has vanished; he is now reckoned simply as a thief.”
“What do you think, Great King?
If this were so, would these four castes be equal, or not?
Or what is your view on this matter?”
“Certainly, Master Kaccāna, this being so, these four castes are exactly equal.
I do not perceive any distinction among them here.
“By this method also, Great King, it should be understood how this is merely a reputation in the world:”
“The brahmin caste alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior … [as before] … they are the heirs of Brahmā.
“What do you think, Great King?
Suppose here a khattiya, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, goes forth from the home life into homelessness…”
“Suppose he had gone forth, abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from false speech, refraining from sexual activity at night,
eating only one meal a day, living a life of celibacy, virtuous, and of beautiful character. What would you do with him?”
“Sir Kaccāna, we would pay homage to him, or rise up for him, or invite him to a seat,
or extend an invitation to him for robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
or we would provide him with righteous protection, defense, and security.”
"And for what reason?
Because, Master Kaccāna, whatever designation he previously had as 'a khattiya' has disappeared; he is now reckoned simply as a 'recluse' (samaṇa).
"What do you think, Great King?"
In this case, a brahmin, a merchant, or a laborer might shave off his hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness;
he would abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, and abstain from false speech;
he would refrain from sexual activity at night, eat only one meal a day, live a life of celibacy, and be virtuous and of good character.
"What would you do with him?
"We would pay homage to him, Master Kaccāna, or rise up for him, or invite him to a seat, or invite him repeatedly;
or we would provide him with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; or we would support him righteously."
“Let us arrange for his protection, defense, and security.
And why is that? Because, Master Kaccāna, whatever former designation he had as a ‘śūdra’ has disappeared; he is now reckoned simply as a ‘monk.’”
“What do you think, great king?
If this were so, would these four castes be equal and the same, or not?
Or what is your view on this matter?”
“Certainly, Master Kaccāna, this being so, these four castes are equal and the same.
I do not perceive any distinction among them here.
“By this method also, Great King, it should be understood how this is merely a reputation in the world:”
‘The brahmin alone is the highest caste; other castes are inferior.
The brahmin alone is the bright caste; other castes are dark.
Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.’
“Brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, heirs of Brahmā.
When this was said, King Mādhura of Avantī said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
“Magnificent, Master Kaccāna! Magnificent, Master Kaccāna!”
"Just as, Master Kaccāna, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Kaccāna in many ways."
“Venerable Kaccāna, I go for refuge to you, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the venerable Kaccāna accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
“Do not go for refuge to me, Great King. It is to the Blessed One that you should go for refuge.”
“Go for refuge to that very Blessed One whom I have gone for refuge.
“But where, Master Kaccāna, does that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell at present?
“Great King, that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has now attained final Nibbāna.”

“Master Kaccāna, even if we were to hear that the Blessed One was ten *yojanas* away, we would travel those ten *yojanas* to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Master Kaccāna,
even if we were to hear that the Blessed One was twenty *yojanas* away,
thirty *yojanas* away, forty *yojanas* away, or fifty *yojanas* away, we would travel even those fifty *yojanas* to see him.”
To see the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Even if we were to hear of that Blessed One from a hundred yojanas away, Master Kaccāna, we would go even a hundred yojanas to see that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
And since, Master Kaccāna, that Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, we go for refuge even to the Blessed One who has attained final Nibbāna, and to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Kaccāna accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The Madhurasutta, the fourth, is finished.
